title: Modern Physics
lines: USAT modern physics questions are short: photon energy and the photoelectric equation, de Broglie wavelength, energy levels of hydrogen, half-life and decay equations, binding energy, and basic electronics (diodes, rectifiers, transistors and logic gates). Know the constants and the one-line formulas, and be ready to work in electronvolts.
## Photons
- Planck: radiation is emitted and absorbed in quanta of energy E = hf = hc/λ, with h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Halving the wavelength doubles the photon energy.
- A useful shortcut: E(eV) ≈ 1,240 ÷ λ(nm). Photon momentum p = h/λ.
## Photoelectric effect
Light above a threshold frequency f₀ ejects electrons from a metal surface instantly.
- Einstein's equation: hf = φ + K(max), where the work function φ = hf₀.
- K(max) = eV₀, where V₀ is the stopping potential.
- Raising the intensity increases the number of electrons but not their maximum energy. Raising the frequency increases their maximum energy.
- Below f₀ no electrons are emitted, however bright the light. This cannot be explained by the wave theory.
> Example 1. Light of photon energy 5.0 eV falls on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons and the stopping potential.
> K(max) = 5.0 − 2.3 = 2.7 eV, so the stopping potential is 2.7 V.
## Other quantum ideas
- Compton effect: an X-ray photon scattered by an electron has a longer wavelength; Δλ = (h/mc)(1 − cos θ). This shows photons carry momentum.
- Pair production: a photon of at least 1.02 MeV (2m₀c² for an electron) can become an electron and a positron near a nucleus. Annihilation is the reverse.
- De Broglie: every moving particle has a wavelength λ = h/p = h/mv. Electron diffraction confirms it, and the electron microscope uses it.
- Uncertainty principle: Δx Δp ≈ h; position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
- Special relativity: moving clocks run slow, moving lengths shrink along the motion, and mass and energy are linked by E = mc².
## The hydrogen atom
- Bohr: the electron moves only in orbits where its angular momentum is nh/2π.
- Energy levels Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV: −13.6, −3.4, −1.51, −0.85 eV … Radius rₙ = n² × 0.053 nm.
- A photon is emitted when the electron drops: hf = E(upper) − E(lower). The ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 eV.
| Series | Final level | Region
| Lyman | n = 1 | ultraviolet
| Balmer | n = 2 | visible
| Paschen | n = 3 | infrared
| Brackett, Pfund | n = 4, 5 | infrared
> Example 2. Find the energy of the photon emitted when a hydrogen electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2.
> E = 13.6(1/2² − 1/4²) = 13.6 × 3/16 = 2.55 eV. It ends on n = 2, so it is a visible Balmer line.
## X-rays and lasers
- X-rays are produced when fast electrons strike a metal target. The shortest wavelength is λ(min) = hc/eV, so a higher tube voltage gives a shorter λ(min).
- The spectrum has a continuous part (braking radiation) and characteristic lines of the target metal.

- LASER means Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation. It needs a population inversion, made possible by a metastable state. Laser light is coherent, monochromatic and nearly parallel.
## The nucleus
- A nucleus ᴬ_Z X has Z protons and A − Z neutrons. Isotopes have the same Z but different A.
- Mass defect Δm = (mass of separate nucleons) − (mass of nucleus). Binding energy = Δm c², and 1 u is equivalent to 931 MeV.
- Binding energy per nucleon measures stability; it peaks near iron-56. Heavy nuclei release energy by fission, light ones by fusion.
- A nuclear reactor uses a moderator (graphite or heavy water) to slow neutrons and control rods (cadmium or boron) to absorb them. Fusion needs temperatures of about 10⁷ K.
## Radioactivity
| Emission | Change in A | Change in Z | Penetration
| α (helium nucleus) | −4 | −2 | stopped by paper
| β⁻ (electron) | 0 | +1 | a few mm of aluminium
| γ (photon) | 0 | 0 | several cm of lead
- Ionising power runs α > β > γ; penetrating power γ > β > α.
- After n half-lives the fraction left is (½)ⁿ. The half-life T½ = 0.693/λ, where λ is the decay constant.
> Example 3. A sample of 64 g of a radioisotope has a half-life of 5 days. How much remains undecayed after 20 days?
> 20 days = 4 half-lives: 64 → 32 → 16 → 8 → 4 g.
! In a decay chain, find the α count from the change in A first; β particles do not change A.
> Example 4. Uranium-238 (Z = 92) decays to lead-206 (Z = 82). How many α and β⁻ particles are emitted?
> α: (238 − 206) ÷ 4 = 8, which lowers Z by 16 to 76. To end at 82, Z must rise by 6, so 6 β⁻ particles are emitted.
## Electronics

- Pure silicon or germanium is an intrinsic semiconductor. Adding a pentavalent impurity (P, As) gives n-type (electrons in majority); a trivalent impurity (B, Ga, Al) gives p-type (holes in majority).

- A p-n junction conducts in forward bias (p side to +) once the barrier is overcome (about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium); in reverse bias the depletion region widens and almost no current flows.
- Half-wave rectification uses one diode; full-wave uses two (centre-tap) or four (bridge). On 50 Hz mains, full-wave output pulses at 100 Hz.
- Transistor: I(E) = I(B) + I(C), current gain β = I(C)/I(B). As an amplifier, the base-emitter junction is forward biased and the base-collector junction reverse biased.
- Logic gates: AND gives 1 only if both inputs are 1; OR if at least one is 1; NOT inverts; NAND and NOR are the inverted forms and are universal gates.
! Brighter light does not give faster photoelectrons, only more of them.
! Compare nuclear stability using binding energy per nucleon, not total binding energy.
## Quick check
- Photon wavelength halved: energy? (doubled)
- Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state? (13.6 eV)
- Which series of hydrogen lies in the visible? (Balmer)
- 1/16 of a sample left: how many half-lives? (4)
- Ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier on 50 Hz? (100 Hz)
